
# Interbranch Representation {#sec-intro}

> ABSTRACT: Contemporary understanding of congressional representation has been limited by a myopic focus on legislative work. Scholars have largely overlooked a significant component of the work of congressional offices: direct engagement with federal agencies. We have thus failed to assess our democracy on important grounds. This chapter introduces a concept of interbranch representation, shows that it is highly unequal, and discusses the implications of highly unequal levels of interbranch representation for democracy. We conclude with a preview of our theoretical framework (demand, capacity, and strategic responses to the political environment) and empirical results of subsequent chapters that seek to explain the reasons for variation in different types of interbranch representation.

In the first few weeks of 2024, the Office of Legislation within the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) received 25 letters from members of Congress. These letters are part of a routine, quiet, but crucial undercurrent of legislative-executive interactions that exists beneath higher-profile hearings and investigations---forms of interactions between Congress and the bureaucracy with which the public is decidedly more familiar. A handful of these letters to the FDA in early 2024 concerned policy, as hearings and investigations usually do. For example, Representative Dan Goldman wrote with concerns about a rule that the FDA had recently proposed to regulate Laboratory Developed Tests (LDTs), and Senator Dick Durbin wrote regarding the FDA's enforcement of the Tobacco Control Act. Most of the other letters, however, were written on behalf of individual constituents. Members of Congress shared correspondence from constituents who were asking for help obtaining necessary medication, asking for more information about drug shortages, drug trials, compassionate use, and obscure treatments for their medical conditions, and, in one case, urging that a canine dental stick product be removed from the market after it led to the death of their dog. 

The personal---and sometimes poignant---stories contained in these letters conjure pictures of constituents trusting legislators and their staff with some of the most significant struggles of their lives. Moreover, they speak to the important role that communications with the bureaucracy can play in congressional representation. These 25 letters are a miniscule fraction of the hundreds of thousands that members of Congress collectively send to federal agencies every year. And other federal agencies receive communications from legislators with similarly major import for constituents. Veterans seek assistance from their legislators with obtaining healthcare and benefits from the Department of Veterans' Affairs (VA), and families seek records of their loved ones' military service from the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Numerous subagencies within the Department of Labor (DOL) handle requests to assist constituents with obtaining workers' compensation payments, back pay, and coverage for medications and medical procedures. Each year, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) within the Department of Homeland Security receives hundreds of thousands of requests to assist legislators' constituents with immigration matters, including student visas, foreign worker authorizations, and requests for asylum. All of these examples show members of Congress engaging in a deeply meaningful form of responsiveness that the public at large rarely has the opportunity to see.

The responsiveness evident through these communications stands in stark contrast to the version of Congress that exists in the minds of a public that disapproves of the institution at a rate of nearly 85%. A majority of survey respondents describe "most members of Congress" as corrupt, out of touch, and catering to special interests.^[https://news.gallup.com/poll/1600/congress-public.aspx] Very little of Congress's behind-the-scenes correspondence with the bureaucracy, however, supports these assumptions. Beyond writing to federal agencies on behalf of individual constituents, legislators write on behalf of small businesses who are seeking help navigating bureaucratic processes like grant applications and worker visas. Legislators also frequently write in support of nonprofit organizations and local governments seeking grants to help improve their communities. Correspondence about policy, even on behalf of entire industries, often concerns routine matters like rulemaking or testimony at hearings. Contrary to what we might assume about communications that take place out of view of the public, this "hidden half of Congress" contains little work that most constituents would find objectionable. 

<!--Rochelle 9/13: probably need more detail here contrasting Comstock and Cruz-->

Potentially concerning, however, is the fact that some members of Congress are much more engaged in its "hidden half" than others. As an example, consider Representative Barbara Comstock (R-VA) and Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX). In 2018 alone, Comstock sent 559 letters to USCIS and 50 to the VA. Cruz, by contrast, sent only 242 letters to USCIS and 4 to the VA in that same year---despite representing over 28 million constituents in the state of Texas to Comstock's 770,000 constituents in Virginia's 10th district. Comstock and Cruz anchor each end of the distribution of the amount of legislators' correspondence with federal agencies. On average, Comstock sent [NUMBER] letters to federal agencies each year, while Cruz sent an average of just [NUMBER]. Together, they also illustrate the central question and puzzle of this book: why do legislators communicate with federal agencies, and why do some of them do so much more of this work than others?

<!--SUMMARY OF OUR CONTRIBUTION --> 
In this book, we argue that these types of substantive representation beyond legislating belong under an overarching concept of *interbranch representation.* We advance, measure, and explain a particular form of interbranch representation: how members of Congress work directly with federal agencies on behalf of various constituencies. Interbranch representation includes casework (constituency service) on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, and businesses as well as oversight of executive branch policymaking and implementation. We show that interbranch representation is common but varies widely across members of Congress: as Comstock and Cruz illustrate, some provide a great deal to their constituents, while others provide almost none. 

To explain why members of Congress engage in interbranch representation, we offer a unified framework that integrates and extends theories rooted in unequal **demand**, unequal legislator **capacity**, and varying **strategic incentives** to invest time and energy in interbranch representation as opposed to other activities like legislating, communications, or fundraising. Theoretically and empirically, the capacity of congressional offices is at the center of this framework. Unequal capacity consistently explains legislators’ interbranch work across a variety of domains. Constituent demand and legislators' strategic incentives play important roles in shaping which constituents are served, but have smaller effects on the amount of interbranch representation that a district receives. The strategic behavior we do see is associated with partisan/ideological and institutional context, not electoral incentives. Overall, our findings show how congressional offices can function akin to a bureaucratic "logic of appropriateness" when providing interbranch representation.

## What is Interbranch Representation?

<!--Rochelle 9/18: should the stuff about why it counts as representation (currently in the theory chapter) go in this section instead??? I feel like Ruth's comments at APSA suggest we need to talk about representation earlier.-->

<!--DEFINITION--> 
Interbranch representation has both broad and specific definitions. Broadly, it involves officials of one branch of government representing their constituents in the decision-making processes of another branch. In this book, we focus on interbranch representation that occurs between the legislative and executive branches of the United States government. Specifically, we examine requests that congressional offices send to federal agencies.^[Other inquiries of interbranch representation could focus on interactions between the legislative and judicial branches by studying amicus briefs that legislators file in court cases. The scope of our inquiry is limited to the legislative-executive form of interbranch representation.] 

<!--PRIOR SCHOLARSHP HAS STUDIED NARROW SLIDES OF THIS KIND OF REPRESENTATION UNDER DIFFERENT NAMES--> 
Scholars have studied parts of interbranch representation under labels including "congressional oversight," "constituency service" [@Fenno1978], "lettermarking" in the context of spending [@MillsKalafHughes2015], "lobbying," "backchannel representation," "backdoor lawmaking," or "policy representation" in the context of agency policymaking [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @RitchieYou2019; @LauterbachRitchie2025], "legislator advocacy" in the context of both constituent and donor service [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023], "interbranch representation" in the context of legislators advising agency working groups [@USDepartmentofJustice2016], and "interbranch representation of protected groups" in the context of descriptive representation in contacts to the bureaucracy [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], or simply "representation" in the context of all types of requests to the bureaucracy [@JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026]. We adopt "interbranch representation" as an umbrella concept to describe all of these kinds of representational activities, not only working group participation or contacts on behalf of descriptive identities, but also work on behalf of any other constituency, donor, business, industry, or district opinion on policy issues with another branch of government. 

In recent years, scholars have begun to obtain snapshots of this work from federal agencies that are, unlike Congress, subject to the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) disclosure requirements. Acquiring these data is difficult, but doing so has yielded important findings on distributive politics [@MillsKalafHughes2015], descriptive representation [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], agency policymaking [@Ritchie2018, and @Ritchie2023], legislative effectiveness [@KalafHughes2023], and money in politics [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]. However, the lack of systematic data across all policy areas and agencies has necessarily limited the range of questions that could be explored with these data.

Our analysis in this book relies on the most comprehensive dataset of legislators' interbranch activities to date. Through 434 Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, we have obtained congressional correspondence logs from every department in the federal bureaucracy except the State Department.^[We filed a FOIA request for the State Department's congressional correspondence logs in 2018 but have not yet received the data due to the department's significant FOIA backlog.] Together, these correspondence logs, which cover 2007 through 2024, capture over half a million instances of contact between members of Congress and federal agencies. Our work hand-coding these data allows us to identify on whose behalf legislators were advocating in each instance of contact.


<!--SCOPE OF INTERBRANCH WORK--> 
<!--Rochelle 9/15: this might be slightly redundant given the examples discussed in the opening anecdote -->
<!--As the examples above illustrate, legislators' direct work with federal agencies is not limited to helping individual constituents. They also help companies, nonprofits, and local governments navigate the federal bureaucracy. In addition to this broadly defined constituency service, legislators work directly with federal agencies on policy issues, including drafting legislation, shaping implementation, and conducting oversight. -->

<!--IT HAS TWO DIMENSIONS--> 
We conceptualize interbranch representation as varying along two dimensions: the constituency represented (e.g., individuals, businesses, nonprofits, or local governments) and the type of representational activity undertaken (e.g., constituency service or policy work). This yields five sub-types of interbranch representation: (1) constituency service work on behalf of individual constituents, (2) constituency service work on behalf of businesses, (3) constituency service work on behalf of local governments or nonprofits, (4) general policy work with federal agencies, and (5) policy work with federal agencies on behalf of specific industries.^[While it is possible to identify policy benefiting particular industries, we created a "general" category for all other policy work because we found it impossible to distinguish policy work done on behalf of individuals, nonprofits, or local governments, which might be described as "public interest" policy work.]

To date, the activities that constitute these five sub-types of interbranch representation have been addressed by separate literatures. Constituency service has mostly been explored as reelection-oriented behavior [@CainFerejohnFiorina1987], and until recently [e.g. @Snyder2024; @Blackwood2026], scholars have paid little attention to its role in representation. Scholarship on interactions between Congress and the executive branch has focused on strategic delegation of policymaking authority and appropriation of funds on the front end [@Arnold1979; @EpsteinOHalloran1999; @KiewietMcCubbins1991] and oversight on the back end [@McCubbinsSchwartz1984]. <!--As a concept, delegation focuses attention on principal-agent dynamics. Oversight scholarship has also focused on principal-agent relationships, with some recent work on descriptive representation [@Minta2011].  While interbranch representation encompasses many forms of oversight, it is broader than activities traditionally considered oversight (e.g., hearings, investigations, sanctions). --> Oversight scholarship focuses on hearings and investigations and rarely in terms of representation [but see @Minta2011]. However, only a small share of congressional interactions with the executive branch rise to the level of hearings and investigations. The vast majority are interventions in the agency's day-to-day operations [see, e.g., @Lowande2018APSR; @LowandePotter2021]. An interbranch representation perspective broadens the concept of oversight to encompass not only occasional hearings and oversight reports prompted by crises and scandals but also daily requests for information and comments on implementation. Overall, the concept of interbranch representation that we advance in this paper unifies constituency service, oversight, and other behaviors within a broader conceptual and empirical framework.

Interbranch representation includes advocacy on a wide range of subjects. Helping immigrants in their dealings with USCIS and veterans in their interactions with the VA are two very common forms of interbranch representation involving individual constituency service.<!--CITE CRS REPORT ON CASES ACT MOST COMMON AGENCIES--> 
<!-- Specifically, these actions might involve helping veterans check the status of their claims with the VA or helping immigrants file necessary forms. Other forms of individual constituency service might involve helping constituents obtain a tax refund with the IRS, helping constituents check their disability rating with the Social Security Administration, and helping workers receive compensation for their injuries from the Department of Labor. -->

The most frequent requests that legislators make on behalf of businesses also involve immigration, as congressional offices help businesses obtain visas for their workers. Legislators also intervene in federal contracts, permits, rate cases, citations, fines, and loans, including loans for the Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business program. While @Powell2023FERC found that members of Congress who receive more campaign donations from energy companies do more work helping energy companies secure permits and profitable rates, this is not the primary kind of corporate service we find. When we looked at who did the most work on behalf of businesses overall, we found progressive Democrat Senator Elizabeth Warren at the top of the list. This was puzzling at first, given past research and our own data showing that Republicans are more likely to represent business interests. Upon closer examination, however, we discovered what put Warren's office on top: the extraordinary amount of work that her office did to help businesses get visas for workers with needed skills.

Interbranch representation on behalf of nonprofit organizations and local governments often involves legislators' writing in support of grant applications or the many other ways that federal funds pass through state and local governments, police and fire departments, and nonprofits like Community Action Agencies. 

Policy work, both generally and on behalf of industries, involves writing with comments on rules, requests for appearances at hearings, the implementation of legislation, and information about specific policy matters. Congressional offices also advocate for disaster declarations and aid and seek information about how appropriated money was spent and how regulatory and personnel decisions were made inside agencies.

<!--Rochelle 9/23: in these next two paragraphs I tried to briefly explain why interbranch representation counts as representation and talk about what our concept can contribute to the literature on representation, but I think I could be much more precise here, idk-->
In all of these instances of interbranch work, members of Congress are clearly engaging in some form of representation. Constituency service is perhaps most obviously a representational activity, as it involves legislators' offices being responsive to constituents' requests for help. Although some recent work has conceptualized constituency service as a key form of representation [@Snyder2024; @Blackwood2026], most work on constituency service has approached it as an activity that can help legislators electorally [e.g. @Fiorina1977; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987]. Although there is, of course, a vast literature on legislators' representation of their constituents' interests through legislative work, there is very little research exploring how legislators provide service to businesses or nonprofit organizations. Even when examining interbranch work as representation, prior studies have focused mostly on a single type of interbranch representation, showing that legislators engage in interbranch representation to represent constituents' needs [@Fiorina1977; @Fenno1978; @MillsKalafHughes2015; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @SnyderJudgeLordPowellGrimmer2025], constituents' policy preferences [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023], shared identity groups [@LowandeRitchieLauterbach2019], or corporate donors [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023].

By conceptualizing interbranch representation as including all five of these sub-types of constituency service and policy work, our book provides a new perspective on how members of Congress provide representation to their districts. Our data allow us to understand legislators' service responsiveness, allocation responsiveness, and policy responsiveness [@EulauKarps1977] as provided through a single activity. Through these communications with federal agencies, members of Congress are providing service to their constituents, helping organizations within their districts obtain grants, and engaging in policy work. Our theory of Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Choices can help illuminate the extent to which legislators are acting as a "delegate" or "trustee" [@Pitkin1967] when providing interbranch representation. A significant role for constituent demand in shaping this work would suggest that legislators are following a delegate model and simply channeling their constituents' demands to the federal bureaucracy. If, however, capacity and strategic choices also matter for interbranch representation, this picture of representation becomes more complicated. Indeed, we do find that the capacity of a legislator's office ultimately governs their ability to meet this demand. Our book therefore reveals one way in which representation can depend on---and potentially be undermined by---the nature of a congressional office. 

<!--Rochelle 9/23: just couldn't find a good place for this sentence (yet?)
Moreover, the relative invisibility of this activity provides an important theoretical contrast to other, more visible forms of representation, which legislators may provide for different reasons. -->


Our data capture the particular instance of contact between congressional offices and federal agencies that occurs as part of interbranch representation. As a whole, however, interbranch representation is an iterative process, and the components of this process inform the theory of this book. Because it involves both constituency service and policy work, much of interbranch representation may begin with a constituent becoming aware of some deficiency in the world and understanding it as a problem---particularly, a problem in which the federal government has a hand in either solving or creating. Second, the individual recognizes that congressional offices can help with this problem. Third, they contact a congressional office, which constitutes the *demand* part of our theory explaining interbranch representation. Fourth, the congressional office processes the request (per their *capacity*) and decides how to handle the request (in accordance with any *strategy* that they may wish to exercise). Finally, for the subset of cases for which such an action is appropriate and desired by the congressional office, the office will contact a federal agency. Our data capture these instances of contact. 

Two other key features of interbranch representation are important to discuss further. First, as established above, legislators have a significant amount of discretion and autonomy in their decisions about engaging in interbranch representation, including where and how to direct these efforts. Party leaders constrain most other activities that legislators undertake, and even other activities where this constraint matters less, like position-taking, are highly public (e.g. Highton and Rocca 2005). Explaining why legislators engage in interbranch representation can therefore provide rich insight into legislative behavior that, given the importance of party and party leadership, previous work has largely been unable to reveal. Second, congressional staff are as important as legislators themselves for the activities that constitute interbranch representation. Staff are crucial for a number of functions in Congress [e.g. @HertelFernandez2019; @MontgomeryNyhan2017; @CrossonEtAl2020], particularly constituent-facing functions like constituency service [@GroseMangumMartin2007; @LandgraveWeller2020]. Similarly, legislators themselves do not personally undertake all of the interbranch representation activities that they perform. Thus, our theory focuses as much on the capacity and other characteristics of the congressional *office* as much as it does on the decisions and characteristics of legislators. 


## Why Study Interbranch Representation? 

Our data make possible new inquiries into congressional behavior, representation, and legislative-executive interactions. We argue that a focus on legislative work in studies of these three areas has limited our understanding of them. By going beyond studying legislative behavior of members of Congress to examine how they engage with the federal bureaucracy to represent various constituencies, this book makes possible major new inquiries into the previously "hidden half of Congress."

Scholarship on how members of the U.S. Congress represent their constituents has focused on legislative activity, including bill sponsorship [@Schiller95; @RoccaGordon2010; @Lazarus2013; @Waggoner2019; @LauterbachHayesWellerBishin2026; @YoelLucasGrossmann2026], roll-call votes [@rohde1991pal; @poolerose1997; @AnsSnySte2001LSQ; @AnsolabehereJones2010; @Wallace2014; @Fowler2026], committee participation [@Hall1987; @Hall1996; @Gamble2007; @EllisWilson2013; @BanGrimmerKaslovskyWest2022], and floor speeches [@MaltzmanSigelman1996; @Hill02; @PearsonDancey2011a; @PearsonDancey2011b; @Kalaf2020]. Importantly, all of these activities are highly visible to scholars, journalists, and constituents. 

<!-- THERE IS A BIAS TOWARD LEGISLATIVE WORK -->

Much more, however, than votes and the text of bills that become law determines how government affects constituents. Federal agencies staffed by career civil servants and political appointees do a large share of policymaking as well as all policy implementation. Agencies make policy to meet the demands of changing technology and social relations, as well as the demands of changing presidential administrations, even when Congress is silent. And when Congress does manage to pass new laws, it inevitably instructs agencies to make and implement new policies. Even federal laws that empower state governments are almost always shaped and overseen by federal agencies. Given the prominent role of federal agencies in modern governance, it makes sense that members of Congress frequently involve themselves in executive-branch policymaking and implementation to help their constituents, advocate for their districts, and advance their policy goals. However, the relative invisibility of this involvement has made it an under-studied part of representation. We have thus failed to assess our democracy on important grounds.

<!--Rochelle 9/15: this paragraph (which I wrote/rewrote from existing text) needs to be cleaned up & made less repetitive -->
Empirical work that seeks to understand why members of Congress make the decisions that they do also focuses on legislative work. Models of legislative decision-making focus almost entirely on decisions about voting on bills [e.g. CITE]. In addition to being only half of what members of Congress actually do, legislative work is an inherently collective activity, in which legislators must build coalitions, gather information, and make decisions by working with other legislators. Such models are therefore inadequate for understanding how legislators engage in activities involving representation, including interbranch representation, which are much more decentralized. As a result of this focus on legislation, appropriations, and oversight hearings, scholars have characterized the modern Congress as centralized [@Rohde1991] and highly partisan [@Lee2009]. But the constituency service and policy work we study here is neither. Unlike legislative activities that are often subject to constraints from party leaders, members of Congress have a great deal of autonomy over the amount and type of interbranch representation that they perform. Understanding why legislators engage in interbranch representation can provide valuable insight into legislators' behavior absent these partisan and institutional constraints. 

<!-- BIAS TOWARD LEGISLATIVE WORK IS A PROBLEM--> 
<!--PEOPLE SAY CONGRESS IS BROKEN--> 
The focus on legislative work in both scholarship and popular media has additional implications for perceptions of Congress as an institution. Congress is consistently described and depicted as an institution engaged in legislating, appropriations, and oversight. Many would say that it is currently performing none of these functions as it should. For years, Congress has been making headlines for appearing unproductive and dysfunctional, particularly according to legislative metrics like the passage of bills.^[See, for example, "How the House Slumped to Historic Lows of Productivity in 2025" (New York Times, January 16, 2026); "Congress set records in 2025, some more dubious than others" (Washington Post, December 24, 2025); "118th Congress to be the most unproductive in decades" (NPR, December 21, 2023); "Congress on Track to be Least Productive in Modern History" (NBC News, July 21, 2014).] Other collective failures, like the unprecedented Motion to Vacate that ended Kevin McCarthy's Speakership in October of 2023 and the longest government shutdown in history that occurred in October and November of 2025, have highlighted Congress's dysfunction to the public. Partisan polarization in Congress has been at an all-time high for over a decade, and although constituents largely approve of their individual legislators, these approval ratings are polarized by party.^[For example, in the 2020 Cooperative Congressional Election Study, 86.3% of respondents who shared their House member's party approved of them, compared to just 36.1% of respondents who did not share their House member's party.]

<!---THIS BIAS EXISTS BECAUSE INTERBRANCH WORK IS HIDDEN-->
<!--IT IS SURPRISINGLY GOOD-->
But running parallel to the gridlocked lawmaking activities is the work that legislative offices do to help constituents navigate the federal bureaucracy and shape executive-branch policymaking. While many members of the public---and certainly the punditry---are aware of Congress's legislative woes, fewer are aware of the other half of the work that congressional offices do behind the scenes to help constituents and shape executive-branch policymaking. Despite the fact that interbranch representation is largely hidden, only a tiny portion of these activities includes normatively suspect activities, like special work on behalf of corporate campaign donors. When we look closely at what congressional offices are doing, the vast majority of legislators' requests, even those on behalf of business interests, are the kinds of things most people would want their representatives doing, suggesting that the institution of Congress is working to represent constituents and influence policy much more than one would think from reading the news.

<!-- OUR CONTRIBUTION: A UNIFIED FRAMEWORK--> 
We gather disparate scholarship into a unified framework of **Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Choices** to explain variation in interbranch representation, integrating and extending theories rooted in unequal demand, unequal legislator (and legislative office) capacity, and varying strategic motivations to invest time and energy in interbranch representation as opposed to other activities like legislating, communications, or fundraising. Prior work has typically studied these activities --- and their explanations --- piecemeal, focusing on one type of activity and a narrower set of causes at a time. To explain variation in different types of interbranch representation, studies have focused on institutional position [@Lowande2018APSR; @LowandePotter2021; @LauterbachRitchie2025; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026], experience [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @Lowande2018APSR; @JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026], or party status and partisan alignment [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023; @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023; @Lowande2018APSR; @Lowande2019; @LauterbachRitchie2025]. Theories also suggest that interbranch representation ought to be driven by ideological alignment and electoral competition [@Fiorina1977; @Rivers1989; @King1991], but these intuitions are largely unsupported by empirical work [@Lowande2018APSR; @Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023]. Our aim in this book is to integrate types of behavior and explanations to provide a more comprehensive assessment of the drivers of interbranch representation. 

<!-- OUR CONTRIBUTION - SOMEWHAT REPETITIVE --> 
<!--Rochelle 9/16: tried to make this less repetitive and to make it fit better in the context of earlier material in this chapter -->
Studying interbranch representation provides a more comprehensive picture of how Congress works and what it does. While focusing on legislative activities and legislators' voting decisions is valuable, this view misses the 16,000 staffers who do most of the work. It also misses that half of that work involves working with or overseeing federal agencies. By refocusing attention on the bulk of the actual work done in legislators' offices^[Recent data on congressional office staffing [@CrossonFurnasLapiraBurgat2021; @CrossonKaslovsky2024data] suggest that approximately 40% are dedicated to constituency service. A significant share of the other 60% are also engaged in interbranch representation such as oversight investigations, hearings, and working with agencies, executive-branch policymaking, or administrative support for both interbranch representation and legislating. Given that most federal policymaking today is made through agency rulemaking, it is reasonable to estimate that at least 20% of legislators’ policy-focused staff time is engaging in inter-branch representation.], we revisit core questions of political science: How should we understand the representative functions of members of Congress? Empirically, what do they do in office? How do we assess the quality of representation? How do the legislative and executive branches interact? Has it changed in recent years? 



<!--FINDINGS --> 
<!--Rochelle 9/16: STILL NEED TO ADD OTHER FINDINGS - I just moved this paragraph from the section below because I thought it worked better here -->
We find that, collectively, members of Congress make over a hundred thousand requests a year directly to executive branch officials. Unconstrained by legislative agendas and party discipline [@Ritchie2023], interbranch representation allows all members of Congress to directly shape the workings of government. However, we find that this work is highly variable --- some members engage in extensive interbranch representation, and others do almost none.


<!-- IMPLICATIONS FOR REPRESENTATION--> 
These findings have implications for the study of representation in Congress, particularly how scholars conceive of the role of congressional staff and the extent to which representation is unconstrained by legislative agendas and party discipline. The role of congressional staff in interbranch work also speaks to how representation can be improved. More generally, because policy implementation is how the public interacts with government and experiences policy effects, the involvement of members of Congress at this stage of the process matters for representation.

## Variation in Interbranch Representation

## Our Theoretical Framework and Key Concepts

<!--Rochelle 9/15: this seems to belong as an intro to the theory section?-->
<!--Interbranch representation can serve a variety of goals and functions for legislators. One of the questions we take up in this book is whether we should think about variation in all of these activities as having a common set of causes or as having distinct causes for different types of interbranch representation.-->

Our framework of Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Responses to the Political Environment extends and unifies theoretical ideas from disparate strands of scholarship on Congress and the bureaucracy.
Demand- and capacity-related explanations focus on congressional offices as bureaucracies, with routines for processing inputs and outputs determined by the allocation of limited capacity, such as staffing levels and expertise. Strategic explanations focus on legislators as politicians, with incentive structures shaped by their political and institutional context. 

**Demand.** We define *Demand* as the constituent-driven influences on a congressional office. In any democratic system, the needs and preferences of a legislator's constituents are supposed to play a role in the work done by a legislator's office. While a large literature exists examining whether and how constituents' policy preferences impact legislators' voting behavior [@MillerStokes1963; @AchenBartels2016], less is known about how constituent demand relates to the provision of interbranch representation.


**Capacity.** We define *Capacity* as the ability of a legislator's office to produce work. We argue that the amount of interbranch representation that legislators engage in is likely to be positively associated with the capacity of the legislator's office. Member offices with greater capacity have the potential to provide more interbranch representation, while the inverse is true for offices with less capacity. We are building on four branches of capacity literature: (1) formal theory voter screening models that predict that as a legislator's capacity increases, they will increase their level of constituency service [@AshworthBuenodeMesquita2006], (2) empirical research that suggests low congressional capacity serves as a major constraint on Congress's work [@LaPiraDrutmanKosar2020; @Reynolds2020; @BoltonThrower2016; @BoltonThrower2022], (3) empirical research that shows legislator capacity impacts backchannel (backdoor) policymaking  ---  when legislators contact executive agencies attempting to influence policy [@Ritchie2018; @Ritchie2023], and (4) our prior research that shows that increases in congressional capacity can offset shifts in legislator priorities between policymaking and constituency service [@JudgeLordPowellGrimmer2026].


**Strategic Responses to the Political Environment.** We define *Strategic Choices* as decisions legislators make about what to prioritize and how to allocate their time and resources in response to the political environment (partisan, electoral, and institutional conditions a member faces in a given year). How much energy and staff time do legislators want to devote to interbranch representational activities as opposed to other tasks like legislating, communicating, and fundraising? Similarly, how much time and energy do they want to devote to different types of interbranch representational activities? We argue that the answer depends on what legislators are trying to accomplish and the political environment that shapes their ability to achieve their goals. Beginning with @Fenno1973 and @Mayhew1974, a substantial body of legislative politics literature has explored the strategic motivations of members of Congress. 

In this book, we examine a variety of strategic choices, drawing on established literatures on reelection motivation [@Fenno1973; @Mayhew1974; @Fiorina1977; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @SerraCover1992; @SerraMoon1994; @DroppPeskowitz2012], ideological motivations [@Lowande2019], obstacles in the legislative process (such as being in the minority party) changing incentives to engage in backdoor policymaking [@Ritchie2023], committee assignments that position members to engage in policy oversight of specific agencies [@Lowande2019; @LowandePotter2021], and being a member of the president’s party shaping anticipated cooperation from the executive branch [@BerryBurdenHowell2010]. 

Notably, several of these strategic motivations provide different expectations for different types of interbranch representation. For example, the substantial body of reelection incentives literature suggests re-election-focused legislators would want to engage in constituency service [e.g., @King1991; @AshworthBuenodeMesquita2006]. On the other hand, Ritchie’s findings in *Backdoor Lawmaking* showed no consistent relationship between electoral vulnerability and policy work with federal agencies [@Ritchie2023]. In this book, we provide both a general theory of interbranch representation and distinct hypotheses for each of our subtypes of interbranch representation. 


## Why Interbranch Representation Matters


### Impact of Federal Bureaucracy on Lives of Americans

In addition to the policy impacts of bureaucratic regulations, which range from vehicle and product safety to the use of REAL IDs, the federal bureaucracy affects the lives of many Americans more directly. Federal agencies administer programs and distribute benefits to millions of Americans. Over 75 million Americans received Social Security benefits in April of 2026. In Fiscal Year 2023, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) processed over 10 million requests and naturalized nearly 900,000 new U.S. citizens. Between 1970 and 2025, the Department of Labor paid over $18 billion in benefits to coal miners suffering from black lung. By keeping seniors out of poverty, by granting citizenship and its rights to immigrants, by compensating coal miners for their illness and suffering, and by administering many similar programs, the federal bureaucracy directly touches individuals' lives in profound ways. The federal government employs over two million civil servants who use their expertise to administer these programs and serve the American public. Recent reductions in the federal workforce by the Trump administration have laid bare the impacts of the federal bureaucracy on regional employment in addition to policy implementation and the delivery of services. And as recent government shutdowns have made clear, many Americans depend on the federal government for a paycheck, in addition to the public's depending on the federal government for basic safety and regulatory measures.

As former member of Congress and political scientist David E. Price described, "Congressional casework often provides a kind of appeals process for bureaucratic decisions, a function that has sometimes been likened to that of the ombudsman in Scandinavian countries. It is not an ideal mechanism... It would be preferable to have all comers receive fair and efficient service from the agencies in the first place" [@Price2022, pg 101]. In an ideal world, as Congressman Price argued, the federal bureaucracy would administer its programs with no errors or delays. Beneficiaries would receive timely responses to their queries, and agencies would have the capacity to handle unexpected surges in demand for assistance. In practice, however, this is not the case. Bureaucratic processes will always be vulnerable to human error, and in such instances, constituents will need help addressing these errors. Although some programs are designed with "administrative burdens" to make them less appealing for the public to use [@HerdMoynihan2019], even minimally burdensome agencies, like the Social Security Administration, can make mistakes that require intervention. Members of Congress, as elected representatives, are well positioned to help their constituents with these problems. And there need not be a bureaucratic error or failure for a constituent to reach out for help: the standard language for casework requests on legislators' official websites makes it clear that constituents can ask for help "if [they] feel [they] have been treated unfairly" in an interaction with a federal agency. Constituency service, then, can say as much about constituents' perceptions of fairness as it can about the functioning of the federal bureaucracy. 

For these and many other reasons, constituent demand for interbranch representation is difficult to measure precisely. But differences in interbranch representation can tell us much about how members of Congress choose to serve their constituents and why some constituents receive more of this help than others. As we discuss in the next section, interbranch representation can also help to inform our understanding of the relationship between the legislative and executive branches.

### Reshaping Our Understanding of How Legislative and Executive Branches Interact

In studying interactions between Congress and the executive branch, political scientists have focused on formal delegation, bargaining over legislation, and oversight hearings. While important, modern scholarship neglects the bulk of how legislators actually interact with the executive branch, which is much less based on formal legal authority and constitutionally prescribed roles that ground most models of interbranch relations. While certainly operating in the shadow of formal oversight, lawmaking, and budgeting powers, interbranch representation mostly relies on norms and softer forms of legitimacy. From an interbranch representation perspective, "separation of powers" is a misleading moniker. The behavior we document involves formal and informal mechanisms by which legislators influence how the executive branch makes and implements policy, but there is little separation. 

Being in the "legislative branch" often prevents us from seeing congressional offices as bureaucracies with functions in the broader system of the U.S. government. 
Including but far beyond "fire alarm" oversight, legislators are involved at every level and stage of bureaucratic politics. There is constant communication between legislators and agencies, including requests tagged as “VIP” that expedite bureaucratic procedures and elevate decisions to higher layers of the federal agency in question. Members of Congress function as a complaint and appeals process for the allocation of benefits, grants, permits, and contracts. They function as powerful allies to advocacy and lobbying campaigns. In short, we should think about congressional offices as part of the network of institutions that make government tick. The functioning of one interacts with the functioning of the other in a broader system of government.
  
<!-- I don't think this bit really responds to Molly's critique 
Congress may appear dysfunctional in many ways, but it is important to note that agencies have not escaped poor public approval, particularly the perception that it is inefficient. The term "red tape" has come to characterize this bureaucratic inefficiency in a wide variety of contexts. 

Originally (and literally) used by 16th-century Spanish officials to bind and identify the most important government documents, "red tape" continued to be used by first the British and then the U.S. governments for similar purposes. Red tape became associated with the burdens of bureaucracy after the Civil War, when U.S. officials used red ribbon to seal veterans' service records. The final step in accessing these records (after the veterans involved traveled to Washington) was physically cutting the ribbons that bound the documents. In the many decades since, "cutting through red tape" has become a well-worn metaphor for reducing bureaucratic inefficiencies. Members of Congress occasionally use this language when discussing constituency service, reinforcing the characterization of the bureaucracy as an inept and complex institution. --> 
While members of Congress are often intervening on behalf of their constituents when they encounter problems with the federal government, we can also think of these interactions more neutrally, as simply one institution filling gaps left by the other. The ability of legislators to connect constituents to a vast and sprawling bureaucracy is valuable both in good times and in bad. Constant, rapid changes in the world lead to changes in how constituents experience the federal government, which necessarily involves some amount of friction with the federal bureaucracy. To fully fulfill its representational duties, Congress should have the capacity to reduce that friction.

Numerous examples from our data illustrate how interbranch representation, especially individual constituency service, is not always undertaken because constituents are experiencing a problem that *originated* in the federal bureaucracy, even though it does *involve* the federal bureaucracy. For instance, Representative Bob Gibbs wrote to the Office of Congressional and Intergovernmental Affairs within the Department of Labor on November 26, 2019 on behalf of a constituent who was having trouble creating an online account as part of the process of permanently hiring a foreign worker. Although some government websites, like HealthCare.gov, have famously experienced widespread problems, other, more idiosyncratic problems are common features of nearly all websites. The difficulty could also have been the result of simple user error. In this case, it is valuable that Gibbs was able to reach out to the relevant agency on the constituent's behalf and provide the kind of representation that would allow them to take this action for their business.

A similar example comes from a letter that Senator Cory Gardner sent to the National Park Service (NPS) within the Department of the Interior on June 9, 2017. Gardner was writing on behalf of a "constituent requesting insurance information from a driver that caused his accident." Presumably, the driver was an employee of the NPS, but aside from that fact, nothing about the constituent's need in this specific incident was unique to a government agency. Requesting insurance information from other drivers is a routine part of handling the aftermath of a car accident. It does not indicate that a bureaucratic process within the NPS is fundamentally broken. In fact, depending on how many similar situations the NPS has experienced, it is possible that they could institute or revise procedures within the agency for dealing with such cases that arise because of unexpected events. 

More generally, our dataset contains a large number of letters, mostly sent to the Department of Veterans' Affairs (VA) and various Department of Labor subagencies, in which constituents are simply requesting the status of the claims that they have filed with these agencies. While these contacts could be the result of a lack of communication from the agency and/or a particularly slow processing speed when it comes to handling claims and requests, they do not appear to be driven entirely by things in the bureaucracy that are fundamentally broken. 

Rather than indicating a fully broken system of government, these interactions between the legislative and executive branches suggest that, holistically, the system can work, especially when it comes to representing constituents. Indeed, studies of congressional oversight of the bureaucracy or the legislative process that ignore the role of interbranch representation are missing potentially important parts of the picture. As Kenneth G. Olson so eloquently describes, 

> "...responding to constituents' complaints and problems provides a recurring opportunity for a member to scrutinize the work of the executive and judicial branches....Characteristically, this scrutiny takes the form of interfering in federal administrative processes on specific issues of complaint. Sometimes such interference goes beyond the individual issue concerned and results in systematic changes in administrative procedures. Occasionally it leads to corrective legislation. In any event, the mere threat of congressional intervention helps ensure that the federal bureaucracy will anticipate problems before they arise and will not neglect its duties. Thus the exercise of the service function infuses new life into the theory of Congress as a check on the other branches of government and as a kind of balance-wheel within the entire system of government." 
>
>----- [@Olson1966, pgs 338-339]

## The "Hidden Half" of the Broken Branch? 

Members of Congress make choices about how much effort to allocate to interbranch representation in terms of both staff and time, as well as which topics and policies to work on and whom to represent. These choices are constrained by their capacity and sometimes driven by events of the day. But unlike other aspects of the job, these choices are not constrained by public attention from either constituents or the media. Rather, these choices are made behind the scenes, and the consequences of those decisions are largely invisible to constituents and journalists. Members of Congress are not required to disclose or report how much constituency service or interbranch representation they have provided. Indeed, as we discovered firsthand, it is exceedingly difficult and time-consuming for academics to track down that information. 

Given the budget constraints and challenges facing journalists today, it is almost unthinkable that a journalist could track down the necessary records to show that Senator X or Congressman Y is one of the worst performing Members of Congress in this regard. Savvy legislators thinking rationally about how to allocate their scarce time and resources may choose to allocate their attention elsewhere into areas that may be more public-facing---such as communications staff or legislative work like introducing bills. They may think carefully about shirking on types of activities that receive media attention, especially votes on bills, which have received more attention of late as a closely divided Congress makes every vote important [@DesjardinsMiduraJackson2026]. 

We argue that interbranch representation is unique because it is invisible---it is work in which legislators engage when the public at large is not looking. This "hidden half of Congress" is difficult for academics to measure, difficult for journalists to cover, and, perhaps most importantly, difficult for voters to monitor. Almost by definition, this is a topic that we know very little about. In contrast to visible forms of representation like roll call voting, bill sponsorship, congressional press releases, and social media posts that have received considerable scholarly attention, invisible forms of representation like constituency service and advocating to the bureaucracy about policy issues have received much less attention. 

<!--All of these visible forms of representation are --- by definition --- known or at least knowable to the public, journalists, and scholars. Politicians know that they are or can be watched or scrutinized based on what actions they take (or fail to take). But what if there is a political equivalent to the Hawthorne Effect in which politicians modify their behavior because they know they are being watched?^[Wikipedia defines the Hawthorne Effect (originally coined in 1953) to be "a type of human behavior reactivity in which individuals modify an aspect of their behavior in response to their awareness of being observed."] Thus, invisible forms of representation might be subject to the absence of a Hawthorne Effect in which politicians know that they are not being watched, and thus behave differently because voters and journalists do not know what they are doing, and thus can neither evaluate their actions nor hold them accountable. -->

Much has been written about Congress as the “Broken Branch” of American government [@mann2006bbc; @LaPiraDrutmanKosar2020]. While explanations for why this is the case have varied, scholars have consistently shown the drop in Congress’s capacity to legislate [@Binder2015]. This literature has largely focused on Congress’s most visible legislative work --- sponsoring bills and casting roll call votes  ---  which have received extensively scholarly scrutiny. Some limited attention has been paid to the public actions of congressional committees, such as roll call votes within committees, committee assignment requests, committee assignments, committee transfers, and passing bills out of committees. Measures of legislative effectiveness are built on these visible actions of representation [@VoldenWiseman2014]. 

Amid the dysfunction that has been apparent in recent Congresses, some observers have noted that the institution nevertheless is capable of passing some legislation, often with bipartisan support. Dubbed the "Secret Congress," this part of the institution receives far less media attention yet appears much more functional and cooperative, thus obscuring the positive legislative work of Congress from public view. Critics of this theory, however, argue that this obfuscation of bipartisan cooperation is detrimental to democracy. From this perspective, constituents' ignorance of this facet of Congress defeats its purpose.

The "hidden half of Congress" that we examine in this book goes far beyond the "Secret Congress" that works well to pass bipartisan legislation. Instead of a more functional version of the legislation-focused Congress with which the public is already familiar, interbranch representation is an altogether different type of work, and many constituents are unaware that Congress is undertaking this work at all. This ignorance of interbranch representation exists despite the fact that it helps to represent constituents and forms a large component of the workload shouldered by congressional offices. By that logic, its obfuscation is even more detrimental to democracy. In what follows, we provide the first evidence systematically documenting interbranch representation and its extraordinary variation. 


<!--In this book, we provide the first evidence systematically documenting the inequality in invisible representation. Our goal is to explain this variation to better understand who Congress represents when no one is watching. When and under what circumstances do members of Congress take action behind the scenes? And when they do act, who are they acting on behalf of: individual constituents, corporations, or nonprofits/local governments? -->


## Organization of the Book

<!--Rochelle 9/18: we need to rewrite this whole section!!! ha ha ha :') -->

In Chapter 2, we review the existing literature on interbranch representation and introduce our unifying framework of Demand, Capacity, and Motivation to conceptually organize explanations for variation in overall levels of interbranch representation as well as each of our five sub-types of interbranch representation. Existing work that focuses on narrower explanations and typically just one of these outcomes misses variation in who is being represented ---  individual constituents, businesses, or nonprofits ---  and the relationship between policy work and constituency service work. These activities are linked, not only because they come from a common budget of effort and time, but also because one often leads to the other. Casework and oversight are more connected than scholarship that studies them separately implies.^[Contrary to the common separation of casework and legislation [e.g., @Reynolds2020, p. 37], we also find evidence of constituency service informing legislation.] Moreover, many activities that fit in our framework (e.g., advocacy on behalf of local governments) are missed by the existing triad of legislation, oversight, and casework representing individual constituents. We explain how our theory builds on existing theories of representation. 

In Chapter 3, we discuss how, up to this point, interbranch representation has been largely invisible to voters, journalists, and scholars, which has consequences for democratic accountability. This chapter briefly describes our approach to measuring and collecting data on interbranch representation. Communications among government officials are, by law, public records. But agencies rarely just post the mail they get from members of Congress online. Thus, we had to file requests for these records under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). We describe the process of translating records from many different agencies into aggregate data on representation activity. We then detail our coding process for determining who was being represented in each case and coding our five sub-types of interbranch representation: 1) constituency service work on behalf of individual constituents, (2) constituency service work on behalf of businesses, (3) constituency service work on behalf of local governments or nonprofits, (4) working directly with federal agencies on general policy issues, and (5) working directly with federal agencies on policy on behalf of specific industries. Finally, we present descriptive tables and figures, documenting staggering levels of inequality in the provision of all types of interbranch representation across legislators (and districts) that motivate the rest of the book.

Chapter 4 presents tests of explanations for overall interbranch representation work using cross-sectional, within-legislator, and within-district differences-in-differences specifications. We find evidence that demand, capacity, and strategic motivation all shape interbranch representation. While capacity plays the largest role, demand in the form of constituent population also plays an important role. We find less evidence of the political environment shaping legislators' strategic choices, with three major exceptions: we see evidence of legislators working with ideologically aligned agencies, strategic staff choice allocations matter --- more constituency service staff results in more interbranch representation (more communications staff results in less). 

Chapter 5 focuses on explaining the unequal levels of constituency service that legislators provide to individuals in their district. Again, we find elements of each part of our Demand, Capacity, and Strategic Choice framework explaining individual constituency service. We find that legislators with more constituents and more demanding constituents (government employees who are better able to advocate for themselves) do more individual constituency service. Similarly, we find that senators who represent more constituents with greater needs also do more individual constituency service, but we do not observe House Members following suit. In terms of capacity, legislator experience again plays a major role; having a seat on a relevant committee with a reporting relationship (oversight jurisdiction) plays a supporting role in some cases, while other more policy-relevant forms of capacity (like committee leadership positions) do not. In terms of strategic choices shaped by the political environment, we see, surprisingly, that neither staff allocation choices nor electoral vulnerability explain the provision of individual constituency service. However, we do observe a surprisingly strong relationship between corporate fundraising and individual constituency service. 

In Chapter 6, we assess explanations for unequal levels of constituency service on behalf of businesses. While demand- and capacity-based explanations again play a major role, strategic motivations play a larger role in explaining legislators' work on behalf of businesses than they do for other forms of interbranch representation. We find that consistent with their pro-business ideological leanings, Republicans do more corporate constituency service. We also find that members of the president’s party do more corporate service work with agencies that they disagree with (are ideologically distant from). Ideologically extreme legislators do less corporate service. Corporate PAC fundraising is associated with corporate service in cross-sectional models.

Chapter 7 aims to explain unequal levels of constituency service work on behalf of specific nonprofits and local governments. Similar to interbranch representation on behalf of businesses, we find that inequality in work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments is mostly a story of unequal capacity across legislators, but constituent demand and legislators' strategic choices play a larger role compared to service on behalf of individuals. Legislators do more for nonprofits and local governments when they have more constituents, and when they have higher-need constituents. Legislators also do much more for nonprofits and local governments when they have a co-partisan in the White House or when they are ideologically aligned with the agency. This fits with research on distributive politics and presidential pork  ---  a story in which nonprofits and local governments are disproportionately served by Democrats, who make requests of left-leaning agencies (like HUD) in Democratic administrations, and Republicans contact right-leaning agencies (like USDA) during Republican administrations. And again, if somewhat counterintuitively, we see a pattern of corporate PAC fundraising being positively correlated with the provision of this form of constituency service. 

In Chapter 8, we shift our focus to inequalities in general policy work that legislators perform as part of interbranch representation. Stark differences in the amount of policy work legislators do are uniquely driven by the capacity gained through institutional positions. Like with other forms of interbranch representation, experience matters, independent of institutional positions of power, but institutional power drives differences in policy work to a degree much greater than any kind of constituency service. Unsurprisingly, being a committee chair, ranking member, or oversight committee member is an especially strong predictor of contacting an agency about policy. Like with constituency service, legislators are more likely to work with agencies on policy when they are ideologically aligned, reflecting how policy work is not just traditional “oversight” investigations into wrongdoing, but also includes proactive information seeking during the drafting of legislation and, most commonly, follow-up to make sure legislative directions result in agency rules as envisioned by the legislators. We also see staff allocation choices matter. Consistent with the notion of interbranch policy work sitting at the intersection of constituency service and legislative work, we find both constituency service spending and legislative staff spending being positively correlated with interbranch policy work. Lastly, we find a different pattern in terms of the role of constituent demand, in which population matters less, but having more college-educated constituents (intense policy demanders) matters more. Again, we find fundraising positively correlated with interbranch policy work. 

In Chapter 9, we examine policy work on behalf of businesses, which is more strategic than general policy work, just as corporate service on behalf of businesses is more about strategic motivation than casework on behalf of individuals. As always, legislator experience plays a central role in shaping the capacity of an office. Like other policy work, chairs, ranking members, and oversight committee members do more. However, policy work on behalf of businesses is distinctly more partisan, with Republicans consistently doing more. Legislators who are more ideologically distant from an agency engage in more policy work with that agency. House Members who are electorally vulnerable do less. Constituent demand plays a more modest role than other types of interbranch representation, with only district population having a relationship with corporate policy work. 

We conclude with a discussion of what our results mean for how we should think about the institution of Congress and the role of legislator offices in a democracy. This includes several analyses of how interbranch representation aligns with other ways of assessing the volume or style of representation, such as Legislative Effectiveness and Legislative Styles. Finally, we look prospectively at the future of interbranch representation, explore the policy implications of our findings for how interbranch representation can be improved, as well as discussing how interbranch representation may be changing during the Trump administration.
